eyebrow: Python for Data Engineers · Chapter 2, Lesson 12
subtitle: Turning date text into real calendar math with datetime.

eyebrow: Why a date needs its own type
code:
# "2026-01-13" > "2026-01-03" happens to return True as plain text,
# but that breaks the moment formats differ or you need real date math.

from datetime import datetime

order_date = datetime(2026, 1, 13)
print(order_date)          # 2026-01-13 00:00:00
print(order_date.year)     # 2026
print(order_date.month)    # 1
print(order_date.day)      # 13
caption: datetime(year, month, day) builds a date directly -- but in real work you're almost always given a date as a string that needs parsing.

eyebrow: strptime() -- parsing a string into a datetime
code:
raw_date = "2026-01-13"
order_date = datetime.strptime(raw_date, "%Y-%m-%d")
print(order_date)         # 2026-01-13 00:00:00

raw_timestamp = "2026-01-13 14:32:07"
event_time = datetime.strptime(raw_timestamp, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
print(event_time)   # 2026-01-13 14:32:07
caption: %Y %m %d match the string piece by piece. Get the format wrong and strptime() raises a ValueError -- immediately useful, not silent garbage.

eyebrow: strftime() -- formatting a datetime back into text
code:
order_date = datetime(2026, 1, 13)

print(order_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))      # 2026-01-13
print(order_date.strftime("%B %d, %Y"))     # January 13, 2026
print(order_date.strftime("%m/%d/%Y"))      # 01/13/2026
caption: The reverse of strptime() -- same format codes, used to display a date to a person or write it out in whatever layout is expected.

code:
first_order = datetime.strptime("2026-01-03", "%Y-%m-%d")
latest_order = datetime.strptime("2026-01-19", "%Y-%m-%d")

days_between = (latest_order - first_order).days
print(days_between)   # 16
caption: Subtracting one datetime from another gives a timedelta -- .days pulls out the span. This is the math behind a real 'incremental load.'
